sentences.text: Borealopelta was an extinct herbivorous ankylosaur that lived during the Lower Cretaceous period in Alberta, Canada.
The generic name combines the Latin word for north with the Greek word for shield, referencing its northern origin and preserved armor.
This animal belongs to the class Ornithischia, a major group of dinosaurs known for their bird-like hips.
It is classified within the family Nodosauridae, which includes other armored dinosaurs like Pawpawsaurus and Europelta.
The fossil shows many tightly packed rows of small bony plates covering the top and sides of its broad body.
This specimen stands out as one of the best-preserved dinosaur fossils of its size ever discovered.
Remarkably, the remains kept their armor in life position, including skin, keratin sheaths, and even stomach contents.
Analysis of melanosomes reveals the animal had a reddish-pink skin tone while alive.
A pair of long spines shaped like bull horns protruded from its shoulders.
The holotype, which is the specimen the species is based on, was uncovered on March 21, 2011.
A miner named Shawn Funk found the fossil at the Millennium Mine, located 30 km north of Fort McMurray.
Caleb Brown and colleagues formally named the species B. markmitchelli in 2017.
The specific name honors Mark Mitchell, who spent over 7,000 hours preparing the holotype.
Stomach contents indicate that ferns were a major part of the animal's diet.
Charcoal found in the stomach suggests it fed in an area recovering from a recent wildfire.
Researchers inferred the animal died only a few hours after ingesting ferns in early or mid-summer.
A flexible keratin layer up to 16 cm thick could withstand forces over 125,000 joules per square meter.
Pigment studies suggest Borealopelta had reddish-brown countershaded coloration for camouflage.
Unlike many relatives, this species had a straight tail instead of a club.
Borealopelta lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, about 110–112 million years ago.
The time range for the genus is the Aptian stage, from 121.4 to 113.2 million years ago.
At the time, the region was covered by the Western Interior Seaway, an inland sea.
The Suncor specimen was preserved in marine sandstones and shales of the Wabiskaw Member of the Clearwater Formation.
The body of Borealopelta must have been washed into the sea by waves, perhaps during a flood.
A siderite concretion formed around the carcass, preventing scavenging and preserving the body intact.

A siderite concretion began forming around the carcass shortly after it reached the sea floor, preventing scavenging and preserving the body intact with its scales and osteoderms in their original configuration.
